summary.text: 院 is used for an enclosed courtyard and in names for institutions. One transmitted analysis builds it from 阜 and 完; another associates it with 寏. Their relationship remains disputed.

formation.text: A transmitted analysis treats 院 as phonosemantic: 阝, the side form of 阜, contributes a wall or enclosure category, while 完 is proposed as the sound element. A competing account treats 院 as a variant of 寏, analyzed with 宀 and 奐. Editorial doubts leave the relation between these accounts unresolved.

components.text: In the 阜-based analysis, 阝 is the positional side form of 阜 (𨸏) and contributes a wall or enclosure category. This component belongs to one disputed construction account.
The transmitted 阜-based analysis identifies 完 as the sound element. Although readings can be compared, they do not independently establish that historical role.

sound_limitation.text: The transmitted account names 完 as the sound element. The supplied reading comparisons are real, but their differences do not independently demonstrate the proposed historical sound relation.

sound.text: The present-day Mandarin readings differ; this pair alone neither establishes nor rules out the proposed historical sound role.
The supplied Middle Chinese transcriptions are comparable but differ; they do not independently establish the proposed sound role.
The reconstructions share some comparable segments but differ in initial, vowel or medial details, and morphology; this comparison alone does not establish the sound role.

history.text: The transmitted tradition preserves two accounts: 阜-based 院, analyzed as 从𨸏完聲, and 宀-based 寏, analyzed as 从宀奐聲, with 院 associated with 寏 as a variant. An editorial proposal questions the transmitted forms and their relationship; the available accounts do not resolve which is earlier.

A seal-style representation is preserved as a modern redraw. The cited Qin manuscript use has no verifiable glyph image here, so the written-form evidence does not provide a complete sequence of changes.

uncertainties.text: The relationship between the 阜-based 院 account and the 宀-based 寏 account remains unresolved.
完 is named as the sound element in one traditional analysis, but the supplied comparisons do not independently establish that historical relation.
The available accounts do not establish a complete graphic sequence or a precise earliest attestation.

senses.text: A cited Qin manuscript passage uses 院 in a context concerning boundaries between lanes and buildings; later glosses equate it with a wall or surrounding wall. This is the earliest use supported here, not proof of the character’s original meaning.
Transmitted literary examples attest 院 in the courtyard sense. The evidence does not establish its first occurrence or a complete development from wall to courtyard.
Transmitted examples use 院 in institutional names and contexts, including an official institution and an academy. They do not establish every step connecting this use to the wall or courtyard senses.
School is a current dictionary gloss. Its first occurrence and development from earlier uses are not established here.

limitations.text: The cited examples support wall or enclosure, courtyard, institution, and school uses, but do not establish precise first occurrences or a continuous sequence connecting them.

overview.text: 院 is commonly used for an enclosed courtyard and in institution names. One traditional analysis assigns 阝 a wall or enclosure role and proposes 完 as a sound element; a competing account links it with 寏, so the earliest construction is unresolved.

components.text: In one traditional analysis, 阝 is the side form of 阜 and contributes a wall or enclosure category.
完 is proposed as the sound element in one traditional analysis, though the comparisons do not independently confirm that role.

relationships.text: In the transmitted 阜-based analysis, 阝 contributes a wall or enclosure category; this is one of two competing construction accounts.
The transmitted 阜-based account identifies 完 as 院’s sound element, but the supplied modern and reconstructed readings do not independently establish the historical relation.
